The Belgian DPA ordered a controller to comply with an access request pursuant to Article 58(2)(c) GDPR. The DPA determined that the controller was responsible for not receiving the data subject's request due to technical problems with its email inbox.
The Danish DPA initiated found that a medical institue could not fail to fulfill its information obligations under Article 14(1) and (4) GDPR with reference to Article 14(5)(b) GDPR.

A new Vodafone prepaid subscriber had expressly objected to the use of his data for marketing. He nevertheless received a parcel of promotional product samples from an advertising company, Chapter Five, to which Vodafone had passed his name, address and phone number. Vodafone argued the parcel was a welcome gift incidental to the contract, not marketing. The Authority found the processing and transfer unlawful, unfair and non-transparent, and incompatible with the original purpose, and that Article 13 information was not shown to have been given. It fined Vodafone EUR 10,000 and ordered it to adapt its practice within one month so that such extra benefits come with full information and a right to object.

A bank customer complained that Piraeus Bank gave a third party, his opponent in a court case, the detailed transactions of two bank accounts he held jointly with his late aunt. The bank admitted that an employee, by mistake and against instructions, handed the data to an heir of the aunt without noticing the accounts were joint and without asking the legal department. The bank did not notify the breach to the Authority or to the customer, arguing that human error is not a breach caused by inadequate security measures. The Authority found breaches of lawfulness and confidentiality principles and of the breach notification and communication duties, and imposed a total fine of EUR 30,000.

Under Article 58(2)(f) GDPR, the Italian DPA imposed a temporary limitation on processing of an AI-powered ChatBot. The privacy policy did not clarify which legal basis had been relied upon by the company, particularly for processing of underage users. The DPA also held that no age verification mechanism was in place.
The use of Cloudflare violates Art. 44 DSGVO.

The DPA held that video surveillance in a shared residential building by one of the co-owner could be based on a legitimate interest in accordance with Article 6(1)(f) GDPR due to the prior unlawful behavior of the other co-owner.

A health authority (ULSS n.5 Polesana) notified a personal data breach: a copy of a patient's medical record handed to him contained 30 pages of another patient's clinical documentation. The Garante found the disclosure of health data had no legal basis and that security measures were inadequate. It took into account that only one patient was affected, the error was human and happened in the Covid emergency, the authority cooperated and acted promptly. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision; no corrective orders were imposed.

A person complained that the hospital authority had sent him a medical report belonging to another patient. The inquiry showed that counter staff of the blood-collection centre were emailing lab reports on request without the encryption and password protection required by the 2013 Prime Ministerial Decree, contrary to the hospital's own instructions. The Garante found the processing of health data unlawful (Arts. 5, 9, 32 GDPR and Art. 75 of the Code) and fined the hospital EUR 7,000, noting the Covid-19 context, its cooperation and its remedial steps. No corrective measures were ordered, and the decision is published in full.

An employee of the municipality of Misterbianco complained that the municipality published on its online notice board a determination, with annexed rankings, on a pay-progression procedure. It disclosed her and other employees' personal data, including details of a labour court judgment and a repayment by salary deductions of up to one fifth. The Garante found the online dissemination had no adequate legal basis and breached the GDPR principles and the Italian Code. It fined the municipality EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

Three individuals complained that a political party had included their names and personal ID numbers in the list of supporters submitted to the Central Election Commission to register for the 4 April 2021 parliamentary elections. Handwriting expert reports found the signatures were not theirs, so the data was processed without consent and without any other Article 6(1) basis. The party did not take part in the proceedings or provide the requested evidence. The Commission found the complaints well founded and fined the party BGN 25,000 for breaching Article 6(1) GDPR. It also ordered the party to adopt organisational measures, training and a data protection policy for breaching Articles 24 and 5(2).

In the context of an erasure request under Article 17 GDPR, the Italian DPA ordered two online newspapers to take action in order to ensure the delisting of their publications from external search engines, insofar as the data subject's name was used as a keyword for the search.

The DPA determined that the controller breached Articles 5(2), 12(2) and 17(1) GDPR, because it was unable to remove the data subject's e-mail from its mailing list. The DPA ordered the controller to comply with the erasure request pursuant of Article 58(2)(c) GDPR.

A complaint was lodged against a company over disclosure of an employee's personal data from his employment contract. In the complaint proceedings the Polish DPA twice asked the company for explanations, and the company never replied. The DPA opened separate ex officio proceedings and found a breach of the duty to cooperate (Art. 31) and of the duty to give the authority information and access (Art. 58(1)(a) and (e)). It imposed a fine of PLN 18,279 (about EUR 4,000). The breach was treated as intentional and continuing, and the company did not respond even to the notice of the fine proceedings.

The Irish DPC conducted an own-volition inquiry into Centric Health after a data breach in which health records of about 70,000 patients became unavailable for two days and records of about 2,500 were permanently deleted. It found that Centric infringed Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2) and 32(1) GDPR through inadequate security measures and failure to demonstrate accountability. The DPC issued a reprimand and three administrative fines totalling €460,000.

The Dutch DPA fined the Social Insurance Institution (SVB) EUR 150,000 for not having appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure personal data in telephone contact with state pension (AOW) clients. The case began with a complaint and a breach notification in 2019, when a relative received a client's information from an SVB employee. The AP found that identity checks and risk assessment were inadequate, and that the infringement ran from 25 May 2018 until June 2022. The standard fine for this category was EUR 310,000. It was lowered because of mitigating circumstances and again, on proportionality grounds, because the SVB acted quickly to fix the problem. No order under penalty was imposed because the infringement had already been ended.

The DPA issued a reprimand against a controller for asking data subjects to provide a copy of their ID as well as signed documents by post, when there were no reasonable grounds to doubt the identity of the data subjects.

Sending an e-mail containing sensitive data with enforced TLS-encryption instead of end-to-end encryption was deemed insufficient secured under Article 32(1) GDPR. The controller received a reprimand instead of a fine as it had increased the security of its communication solutions.

In the context of an erasure request, requiring copy of identity documents which are not strictly necessary to identify a data subject breaches Article 12(6) GDPR. Moreover, in these cases, the use of regular mail does not facilitate the exercise of data subjects' right under Article 12(2) GDPR.

The Polish DPA imposed a ca. €6,387 fine on a district court for lack of adequate security measures which resulted in the loss of three USB memory sticks containing draft judgements and personal data of an unidentified number of data subjects.

The Belgian DPA determined that a controller breached Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 17(1) GDPR by not responding an erasure request. The DPA ordered the controller to comply with the request pursuant of Article 58(2)(c) GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined a private detective €2,000 because of a violation of Article 13 GDPR. The data subject was not informed how her personal data would be processed. The website of the detective, which was referred to in the contract with the data subject, lacked a privacy notice.
The Italian DPA ordered a newspaper to stop the processing of medical data concerning a notorious mafia boss. Journalism shall respect the principle of essentiality of information.
The Italian DPA ordered a newspaper to stop the processing of medical data concerning a notorious mafia boss. Journalism shall respect the principle of essentiality of information.

The Italian DPA ordered a newspaper to stop the processing of medical data concerning a notorious mafia boss. Journalism shall respect the principle of essentiality of information.

After circulating a survery to parents regarding changes to learning and teaching in the COVID-19 pandemic, a pre-school was found to have violated Articles 5, 12 and 13 GDPR. The investigation discovered that it was not made clear whether returning the form was mandatory, and information specifying the legal basis for processing of personal data was not provided.

The DPA found that a controller lacked a legal basis to transfer a data subject's phone number to another telecommunications operator without the data subject's prior authorisation. The DPA fined the controller €1,024 (BGN 2,000).
The Swedish DPA fined the medical board of Region Darlana approximately €1.800 on for breaching Article 32(1) when summoning patients to healthcare appointments by mail.
The DPA fined a controller BGN 2,000 (€1,022) for unlawful transfer of personal data to another controller caused by lack of appropriate organisational and technical measures under Article 24 GDPR.
The Irish DPA fined Kildare County Council €50,000 for unlawful processing of personal data using CCTV cameras, a lack of transparency, and inadequate security measures.

The complainant in the case at hand (the husband) incurred an obligation to disclose his assets as well as income to his wife as a beneficiary of maintenance in the course of divorce proceedings. This did not lead to a violation of the complainant's right to confidentiality by the processing of his personal data.
The Cypriot DPA issued a fine of €7,000 against a local newspaper for violating Article 5(1)(c) GDPR and Article 6 GDPR. The newspaper published names and photographs of police officers on duty.

After press reports of spyware being used to monitor phones in Greece, the authority opened an investigation and carried out on-site inspections at the offices of Intellexa S.A., a company linked in the press to the Predator spyware. The registered office had no real operations and the second site was an empty building. The authority sent 24 written questions, but the company did not answer for over 40 days, and then only partly, leaving out information it plainly held. The authority found a breach of Article 31 GDPR (duty to cooperate with the supervisory authority), fined the company EUR 50,000 and ordered it to hand over the invoices, the material sent to the National Transparency Authority and its relevant contracts straight away.

The Irish DPC announced the conclusion of its inquiry into WhatsApp Ireland, started by a complaint from a German data subject about 'forced consent' to updated Terms of Service. Following an EDPB binding determination of 5 December 2022, the DPC's final decision of 12 January 2023 found WhatsApp could not rely on the contract legal basis for service improvement and security, and also found transparency breaches (Articles 12, 13(1)(c) and 5(1)(a)). It fined WhatsApp Ireland €5.5 million for the Article 6(1) breach, no further fine being imposed for transparency as €225 million had already been imposed earlier. WhatsApp must bring its processing into compliance within six months. The complaint's forced-consent aspect was rejected.

The Latvian DPA ordered a website to delete information about more than 13,000 people whose data were scraped online from publicly available sources, considering that the processing violated the principle of purpose limitation.
A local health authority in Italy failed to respond to an access request made by a data subject, who sought to understand why incorrect data appeared on her covid-19 vaccination certificate.

A teacher complained that the regional school office's Brescia branch published on its website a transfer decision containing personal information and the reason for his priority in mobility, namely assistance to a family member under Law 104/1992, which reveals health information. The office blacked out the health reference after the request but left the decision itself online with the teacher's data. The Garante found publication (dissemination) without a legal basis and in breach of lawfulness, minimisation and the ban on disseminating health data. It fined the office EUR 6,000, restricted further online dissemination of the complainant's data, required a report within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A hospital-university trust in Padua sent an email to 19 heart-transplant waiting-list patients, asking for consent to a clinical study, with all addresses visible in the cc field instead of bcc. This revealed to each recipient that the others were patients awaiting a heart transplant. The trust notified the breach itself. The Garante found unlawful disclosure of health data in breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR and fined the trust EUR 5,000. It imposed no corrective measures because the trust had already acted, and ordered publication of the decision.

A woman who had been involved in failed acquisition talks with the company complained that her individual business email account stayed active after the relationship ended and was accessed. The company kept the account open, forwarded incoming mail to its sales director and deactivated it only at the end of February 2019, citing its interest in serving prospective clients and in defending itself in a civil case. The Garante found the processing unlawful and the reply to her deletion request inadequate, breaching the principles of lawfulness, fairness and minimisation, the legal basis requirements, and the rules on transparency and data subject rights. It fined the company EUR 5,000 and ordered publication. The charges under Article 88 GDPR and Articles 113 and 114 of the Code were dropped.

The Garante inspected Commify Italia, which runs the Skebby SMS platform, in November 2021. It found the company kept the content of customers' SMS messages (including OTPs, health and political messages) without a valid legal basis, had weak security for traffic data (single-factor authentication, http API endpoints, no logging of operations on the systems), and scanned message content for fraud. It fined the company EUR 80,000 under the Art. 83(5) cap, issued two reprimands for the fraud scanning and for the Art. 25 failings, and ordered publication of the decision.
The Italian DPA ordered Google LLC to remove URLs linking to content concerning a former politician due to the harm they caused him personally and professionally.

A magistrate who is a member of the National Association of Magistrates complained that the association sent a confidential notice of internal disciplinary proceedings to the general certified email address of the prosecutor's office where he works, rather than his personal address. Staff of the office therefore saw the information and it was handed to him by hand. The Garante found a breach of the integrity and confidentiality principle and of Articles 25 and 32. It fined the association EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but did not impose a corrective order because the association had already changed its practice.

After Google failed to respond to a right to erasure request made by a Greek data subject, the Greek DPA held that it is competent to examine the complaint, as the processing concerns only a Greek data subject, and is conducted by Google LLC, based in the US.

The Catalan DPA found that the principles of GDPR do not limit the right to access public information on the number of gender transition cases in Catalonia broken down by sex, age, and year because of the efficient anonymisation of the data.

The DPA found that the principle of accuracy does not always impose an obligation on the controller to keep data updated. Completeness is required only when it is necessary to fulfil the purpose of the processing.

The Norwegian DPA reprimanded the Church of Norway for unlawfully collecting information on members' newborns after their legal basis for such processing had expired, and for failing to provide sufficient information as per Articles 14(1)(d), 14(2)(f) and 12(1) GDPR.

The Norwegian DPA held that a courier and logistics company violated Article 32 GDPR for insufficient risk assessment and the lack of security measures in the app MyPostNord, which used phone numbers as the only means of authentication to access a customer profile.

The Spanish DPA issued a reprimand and determined that the Island Council of El Hierro adjust the publications on its transparency portal, reconciling its obligation to publish acts of public interest with the protection of personal data.

A newspaper article reports that the Sachsen-Anhalt data protection commissioner fined Magdeburg University Hospital EUR 9,000 for concealing serious data protection violations. An employee is said to have misused the hospital's access to population registers to retrieve personal data of uninvolved people. The hospital board kept this from the authority for over a year. A further EUR 450 was charged for the costs of the proceedings. The article is paywalled, so only the opening paragraphs are available.
Following a complaint filed by an Austrian Facebook user, the Irish DPA found Meta IE’s processing of personal data for behavioral advertising to be unlawful, and fined the company €210 million.
Following a complaint filed by a Belgian Instagram user, the Irish DPA found Meta IE’s processing of personal data for behavioral advertising to be unlawful, and fined the company €180,000,000.

The Polish DPA was handling a complaint about disclosure of a complainant's data to unauthorised parties by a financial intermediation company. The company did not collect two registered letters requesting explanations, nor answer the letter opening the fine proceedings or a phone call with its president. The DPA opened proceedings on its own initiative and found a breach of Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR for failing to give it the information it needed. It imposed a fine of PLN 27,418 (stated as equal to EUR 6,000), treating the breach as intentional, continuing and a repeat of earlier non-cooperation that had drawn a reprimand.

The French DPA fined Apple Distribution International €8,000,000. Apple implemented its advertising identifiers on Apple devices without prior consent from French users, in violation of Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act.

The French DPA fined VOODOO, a mobile game developer, €3,000,000 for violating Article 82 of the French data protection act. VOODOO did not collect the consent of users for personalised advertising and provided misleading information regarding tracking behaviour of users.
The French DPA fined TikTok €5,000,000 for implementing advertising identifiers on users' devices without prior consent. TikTok's cookie banner was also found insufficiently informative.

The Spanish DPA fined an electricity and gas company €24,000 for the lack of a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR to process the personal data of its client which was caused by an internal error in registering the data subject's will to enter into contract.

In a procedure pursuant to Article 60 GDPR, the Finnish DPA imposed a €122,000 fine on a manufacturer of heart rate monitors due to lack of valid consent for the processing of personal data, including health data, on its online service.
The Maltese DPA found that a controller failed to react to an access request within one month as the GDPR foresees, and failed to provide the data subject with a copy of their personal data.

The Belgian DPA ordered a human resources provider to comply with an access request. In light of the the accountability principle of Article 5(2) GDPR this includes certain information regarding the source of personal data.

The Danish DPA found that Securitas A/S had a legal basis under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR for disclosing the personal data of an employee to the Police Intelligence Service and the Defense Intelligence Service in connection with a security clearance.

Romania's data protection authority concluded an investigation into a broker company in November 2022. An Excel record holding clients' personal data, including ID numbers and bank details, was published online by the company's administrator, exposing the data of at least 509 people. The company was fined RON 49,418 (about EUR 10,000) for failing to ensure that persons acting under its authority process data only on its instructions (Art. 32(4) GDPR). It received warnings for not informing the data subjects of the breach (Art. 34 GDPR) and for storing non-essential cookies without consent (Art. 4(5) of Law 506/2004).

The Icelandic DPA rejected a complaint concerning an alleged unlawful disclosure of personal data by a public authority. The authority had been legally obliged to share the data based on the applicable freedom of information law.

Following a lack of substantive feedback or assessment from the DPC during the mutual assistance procedure (Article 61 GDPR), The Italian DPA initiated the urgency mechanism in Article 66 GDPR to prohibit Meta’s processing of personal data in the context of the Italian elections.
The Hungarian DPA investigated the use of a surveillance camera sytem and fined the controller HUF 3,000,000.00 (approx. €8,000.00) for violating multiple GDPR provisions.

The Bulgarian DPA fined a doctor BGN 500 (approx. €255) for a violation of Article 32 GDPR. The Doctor had allowed that her electronic signature was used to access the vaccination status of a member of the European Parliament. This information was later disclosed in a television programme.
The Greek DPA found that a polling company had violated Articles 12 and 15 GDPR, for failing to respond to an access request submitted by a participant in a telephone survey.
The French DPA fined Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited €60,000,000 for its website "bing.com" through which it had installed non-essential cookies without valid consent.

The Danish DPA held that a controller breached Article 6(1) GDPR by informing the entire workplace about the reasons that led to the data subject's dismissal from the company because the processing went further than what was necessary.

A customer of a slimming and aesthetics business complained that the company ignored her written and extrajudicial requests for copies of her contracts, records of sessions attended and a statement of her surplus balance. The company also failed to answer the Authority's repeated requests for its views over more than a year, replying only after a hearing. The Authority found that access was granted late and incompletely (Articles 12(3) and 15) and that the company breached the duty to cooperate (Article 31). It fined the company EUR 2,000 and EUR 5,000 respectively and ordered it to satisfy the outstanding access request.
A TV show correctly invoked artistic freedom under Article 17(3)(a) GDPR in order to dismiss an erasure request.

The Dutch DPA (AP) reprimanded CAK, a Dutch public body, for violation of Article 12(3) GDPR because CAK did not respond in a timely manner to an access request. The AP concluded a reprimand is a fitting sanction since the breach was small.

The Austrian DPA dismissed a complaint of a data subject against an embassy on the Austrian territory due to a lack in authority pursuant to Article 55(2) GDPR and the diplomatic immunity enshrined in international law.

The Romanian DPA closed an investigation in November 2022 into Societatea Energetică Electrica S.A., which started after the company notified a personal data breach. It found a violation of Article 28(3)(a) GDPR and fined the company 24,654.50 lei (about EUR 5,000). It also recommended that the controller take all necessary measures to comply with Articles 46-49 GDPR on transfers. The text is a short press release, not the full decision.

A patient complained that at the Recoletas clinic in Ponferrada the data-protection consent boxes on the admission tablet (third-party sharing and marketing) were pre-ticked by staff. He also complained that he never received a copy of the form he signed. The AEPD opened sanction proceedings and proposed two fines of EUR 10,000 each, one for Article 6(1) GDPR (defective consent) and one for Article 15 with Article 12 GDPR (no access to the signed document). The hospital paid EUR 16,000 on 31 October 2022 using the 20% reduction for voluntary payment, which ended the procedure. By paying it waived any administrative appeal.

The Garante investigated the stratification of patients by risk (using the Johns Hopkins ACG algorithm, RUB 4 and 5 classes) carried out under a regional resolution for Covid-19 proactive medicine, with lists sent to general practitioners. Health data of over 40,000 patients, 9,487 of them from the Friuli Occidentale health authority, were processed. The Garante found no valid legal basis, no specific information to data subjects and no data protection impact assessment. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the authority EUR 55,000 and ordered deletion of the resulting data within 90 days. A later note says the Tribunal of Pordenone annulled the decision on 13 October 2023.

The Garante investigated a Friuli Venezia Giulia regional programme in which patients were stratified by an algorithm (Johns Hopkins ACG, RUB 4 and 5 risk classes) using health data and lists were given to general practitioners for Covid-19 'medicina d'iniziativa'. About 40,000 patients were involved, 9,487 of them from the Friuli Occidentale health authority. The Garante found there was no suitable legal basis, that patients were not given the Article 14 information, and that no data protection impact assessment was done. It fined the authority EUR 55,000 and ordered it to delete the data resulting from the processing within 90 days. A note says the Tribunal of Pordenone annulled the decision on 13 October 2023.

The Italian DPA fined a health authority €55,000 for the unlawful processing of special category health data. The controller sought to compile a list of patients vulnerable to major complications from Covid-19 infection.

The municipality of Borgia informed the Garante that it was installing fingerprint-based systems to record employee attendance. The Garante found that it had processed employees' biometric data without a valid legal basis, contrary to the principle of lawfulness, and had failed to notify the Garante of the new data protection officer's contact details. The processing was a short trial of three days involving about 13 employees, and the system had been dismantled. Taking into account the small size of the municipality, its cooperation and its good faith, the Garante imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered since the conduct had ended.

A former municipal employee complained that the Municipality of Bracciano published on its online notice board a resolution taking note of her resignation and waiving the notice period. It identified her by initials, job role and employee number and referred to her health condition and drug therapy. The Garante found that this amounted to dissemination of personal and health data without a legal basis, and that initials plus context do not anonymise. It rejected the transparency-law justification. It declared the processing unlawful and fined the municipality EUR 6,000, with publication of the decision.

A lorry driver complained that he found a Visirun GPS tracker in his lorry, installed under a former employer's contract, and that his access request went unanswered. The Garante found that Verizon Connect Italy, the vehicle-tracking provider and processor, never had a written processor appointment under Article 28 with its customer, and that the location processing was unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 28. The processing ran from February 2016 to the end of 2020 and covered 76 devices. The Garante fined the company EUR 30,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

Following several complaints and reports about unwanted marketing calls made on behalf of Edison Energia, the Garante inspected the company in February 2022 and examined its telemarketing and profiling practices. It found that Edison used third-party contact lists without checks on consent, handled objections to marketing poorly (an incomplete do-not-contact list), and collected a single bundled consent for marketing and profiling on its website and app. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, banned further processing based on third-party lists lacking valid consent, and ordered corrective measures on checks, data subject rights and privacy notices. It fined the company EUR 4,900,000, equal to 0.1% of its latest turnover, and ordered publication of the decision.

A patient complained that an emergency-room record at the Policlinico Casilino, run by Eurosanità, was wrongly linked to a namesake patient with a different birth date, and the record ended up with the namesake. The company also notified a data breach. The Garante found that health data of both patients were processed unlawfully, breaching the principles of accuracy and integrity/confidentiality, Article 9 and Article 32 GDPR. It fined the company and ordered publication of the decision. The Rome Tribunal later reduced the fine to EUR 30,000 and upheld the publication (judgment 2648/2025 of 19 February 2025); the Garante's published text shows only the reduced amount.

An Italian doctor made critical statements concerning covid-19 health measures. The Rome Provincial Order of Surgeons communicated, on TV and in a press release, information regarding disciplinary action against the doctor. The Italian DPA reprimanded the Order for violating Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 GDPR.

A delivery driver working for the furniture company complained that he found a GPS tracking device in the engine compartment of his truck, installed without information or valid consent. The Garante found that the company, as controller, processed location and mileage data of identifiable drivers through a device supplied by a telematics provider from 2016 to late 2020, even after the complainant's relationship ended. It found violations of transparency and lawfulness principles, the duty to inform, the processor-appointment requirement and the DPIA obligation. It fined the company EUR 50,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Greek DPA determined that the processing of personal data using a video surveillance camera in an apartment building was unlawful, after the general assembly of owners requested the removal of the device.

According to the Icelandic DPA, in case of legal obligation to carry out a certain processing operation, controllers must assess the law requirements diligently before taking any action. In this case, a bank should have verified the accuracy of information available in some official registration books before disclosing the data subject's data to third parties.

The Luxemburg DPA fined Є3,700 to a company running a website and a mobile app for not providing sufficient information about the processing of data and for using a privacy policy that did not reflect reality.
DPA imposed a fine of 750,000 euros for Alektum Oy for declining data subjects to review their information.

The Luxembourg DPA fined the building manager of a co-ownership property €1,500 for communicating accounting data and private addresses of some co-owners to the other co-owners to warn them about payment irregularities.

The Finnish DPA held that four cities in Finland had, among others, unlawfully transferred personal data to the US when using Google Analytics and Google Tag Manager on their public library online services. The DPA ordered them to delete the data collected through these tools.

Following the notification of a data breach, which gave unauthorized parties access to bank details, the Romanian DPA investigated a controller, concluded that it was in breach of Article 25 and 32 GDPR based on its lacking security measures, ordered the controller to take corrective measures, and fined the controller 9,883.60 RON (equivalent to €2000).

The Finnish DPA fined a shipping company €230,000 for several violations in processing employees' health data, including, among other things, the principles of transparency, accuracy, the right to be informed, the right to access, and the data protection by design.
The Estonian DPA ordered a controller to comply with an erasure request under Article 17 GDPR to delete a former work email address.

The Estonian DPA held that using CCTV cameras to monitor employees cannot be based on consent, but only on legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR provided that a valid interest assessment had been carried out.
According to the Estonian DPA, the publication of debtor's personal data on social media by a debt collection company did not have a valid legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR.
Following a referral under the Article 60 GDPR procedure, the EDPB issued a binding decision finding Meta IE’s processing of personal data for behavioural advertising to be unlawful.
Following a referral under the Article 60 GDPR procedure, the EDPB issued a binding decision finding Meta IE’s processing of personal data for behavioural advertising to be unlawful.

Following a referral under the Article 60 GDPR procedure, on a case initiated by noyb, the EDPB issued a binding decision finding Whatsapp IE’s processing of personal data for “service improvements” and “security” to be unlawful.

The Icelandic DPA decided that a social service had a legal obligation to share sensitive personal data of a mother and her oldest child with the father of the oldest child. The processing was in compliance with Article 6(1)(c) and 9(2)(h) GDPR. However, also sharing the details of the women's other children violated the GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA rejected a complaint of a data subject which demanded the enforcement of the data subject's right to erasure against a controller's genealogical database. The DPA decided that the controller's processing was justified pursuant to Article 6(1)(f) GDPR and that it was within its rights to refuse the erasure request pursuant to Article 17(3) GDPR.

According to the Bulgarian DPA, a company violated Article 6(1) GDPR by sending pre-employment arrangements to a government agency while national law only required them to share finalised employment contracts.

The Italian DPA fined the Lazio Region EUR 100,000 for monitoring the email metadata of staff in the regional legal department (avvocatura), including those writing to a specific trade union. The data was kept for 180 days for generic IT security purposes and used without a proper legal basis, breaching data protection principles and the rules on remote monitoring of workers. The Region said it ran an internal check over a suspected leak of confidential information. The Garante also banned further processing of such metadata and ordered deletion of what was unlawfully collected. This is a press release; the decision itself (1 December 2022) is a separate document.

After a municipal police report and a Guardia di Finanza inspection, the Garante found that two grocery shops in Modena ran working CCTV cameras without information signs and without the labour-inspectorate authorisation or union agreement required for cameras that can monitor employees. The owner also failed to answer the Garante's requests for information. Her defence that she acted in good faith and later put up signs and applied for authorisation was not backed by any documents. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, fined the sole trader EUR 6,000 and ordered her to bring the processing into compliance within 60 days. The decision is to be published.

An employee of a hospital company complained that two of its resolutions, one containing his disability status (health data), were published on the institutional website's online notice board and indexed by search engines. The Garante found no legal basis for disseminating the data and noted the ban on disseminating health data. The publication also ran beyond the 15-day limit, partly because of a platform bug. It declared the processing unlawful and fined the company EUR 6,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

A former employee of Amazon Italia Logistica complained that the company never answered his access request for professional training certificates held from his employment. The company replied only after the Garante opened its investigation, sending the one certificate it could obtain and explaining that the others did not exist. The Garante rejected the company's excuses (request did not cite Article 15, a dedicated email address was not used, summer holidays) and found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The French DPA fined a telecommunications provider €300,000 for several GDPR violations. Among other things, the DPA rejected that the controller's sources of personal data were deemed "business secrets" and held that the controller failed to adequately respond to access and erasure requests.

The Polish DPA imposed a €9,738 fine on a law firm for unlawfully processing personal data of potential clients, including data relating to health, in violation of Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1) and 9(2) GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA held that a provider of a digital signature and verification service violated Articles 5(1) and 6(1) GDPR by processing a data subject's email address and social security number, respectively, without valid consent and contrary to the principle of data minimisation.

The Irish DPC announced the conclusion of its inquiry into Meta Platforms Ireland, controller of Facebook, following media reports of a scraped dataset of Facebook personal data published online. The inquiry examined Facebook Search, Messenger Contact Importer and Instagram Contact Importer between May 2018 and September 2019 for compliance with data protection by design and default. The decision, adopted on 25 November 2022, found infringements of Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR. It imposed a reprimand, an order to bring processing into compliance through specified remedial actions within a set timeframe, and administrative fines totalling €265 million.

The Belgian DPA warned a real estate agency for failing to respond to an erasure request and an objection request. The controller did not remove an advertisement for the property sold to the data subject after the purchase was already completed.
The National Commission on Informatics and Liberty imposed a fine of € 600, 000 on Electricité de France for breaches of Article 7, 12, 13, 14, 15, 21, and 32 of the GDPR.

A customer complained that the electricity distributor Areti wrongly flagged him as a defaulting customer (CMOR indemnity) in the integrated information system, and that his access request was answered inadequately. The Garante investigated and found that a faulty data-extraction query and an erroneous data migration produced inaccurate data for thousands of people over about five years. It found breaches of the accuracy and storage limitation principles, accountability, transparency/access rights and controller obligations. It fined Areti EUR 1,000,000 and ordered it to correct the wrongly migrated data and annotate the records.

A sports-medicine clinic told a gym, where the complainant had enrolled, that her non-competitive sports fitness certificate was suspended pending further tests. The gym then denied her access. The Garante held that this news reveals health information and was disclosed without a legal basis or the complainant's consent, breaching Articles 5 and 9 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ended and a DPO had been appointed.

The Icelandic DPA held that a controller did not violate the GDPR by storing the data subject's phone number in its database because their legitimate interest in research outweighed the interests of the data subject. Moreover, the controller could rely on the exception of Article 14(b)(5) GDPR to not inform their data subjects about the processing of personal data as this would have caused excessive costs.

The Icelandic DPA rejected a data subject's complaint. It held that the controller had a legal obligation pursuant to Article 6(1)(c) GDPR to process her data and that it did not have to inform her about the processing of their personal data pursuant to Article 14 GDPR as it was not received by a third party.

The Icelandic DPA held that a school administrator did not breach the GDPR when sharing the teaching evaluation of a data subject with other staff in a meeting, as the administrator could base the processing on Article 6(1)(c) GDPR and did not share the data with any unauthorized parties.
The Belgian DPA closed the procedure because of a prior settlement decision between the DPA and a press organisation regarding the use of cookies

The DPA dismissed the complaint because the complainant’s data was deemed ‘generally available’ and the respondent’s processing thereof was justified by their legal mandate to efficiently place workers and provide labour market information.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in October 2022 into ING Bank NV Amsterdam Bucharest Branch, started after the bank notified a personal data breach. Customer data, including identity, contact and banking details and Internet Banking credentials, were accessed and disclosed without authorisation, and third parties made payment operations. The authority found the bank had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures, in breach of Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It imposed a fine of RON 98,076, equal to EUR 20,000, which was paid. The press release also says Raiffeisen Bank SA paid its fine.
The Belgian DPA ordered a Covid-19 contact tracking centre to answer an access request, to which the centre did not reply.
The Romanian DPA fined the President of an Association of Owners €300 for not providing the information requested by the DPA by the legal deadline.

During the COVID-19 emergency in spring 2020, two camera cars were used in Rotterdam to monitor and enforce corona rules, filming public spaces including identifiable adults and children. The police chief had not carried out a data protection impact assessment before the processing began; a pre-assessment concluding none was needed was only adopted on 10 May 2020, and the actual assessment on 26 May 2020, while filming continued. The Dutch DPA found a breach of Article 4c(1) of the Police Data Act. It set a fine of EUR 50,000, reduced from the base amount of EUR 56,500 because of the exceptional crisis circumstances at the start of the pandemic.

The Belgian DPA reprimands a government agency for not proactively involving its DPO in a processing activity relying on Article 6(1)(c) GDPR. All processing activities must be in line with the GDPR, even those mandated by legislation predating the GDPR.
